screens.title: Introduction to Materials and Textures
screens.narratorSegment: In this short unit we will build a practical understanding of Materials and Textures in Unity and why they matter for visual fidelity. Materials act as the skin for your 3D meshes and define how light interacts with each surface. You will see how Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, relies on physical properties like metallicness and smoothness to produce consistent results across lighting setups. We will also cover the key texture maps used in PBR — Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness or Roughness, Normal, and Ambient Occlusion — and how to import and assign them correctly. A concrete example you will practice is creating a PBR material for a cube, importing a Normal map and setting its texture type correctly so the surface shading reads properly. A common mistake to avoid is leaving a Normal map as a default texture type, which breaks lighting. By the end you will be able to configure the Standard Shader and apply materials so your assets react correctly to light. Ready to explore material properties and practice a hands-on setup?

screens.title: What Is a Material in Unity?
screens.narratorSegment: A Material in Unity is an asset that describes surface appearance by defining how light interacts with a mesh. Think of the mesh as the shape and the material as the skin: one provides geometry, the other provides color, reflectivity, and micro-detail. A clear definition helps you separate responsibilities in an art pipeline. For example, the same wood texture material can be applied to many models so a set of crates, fences, and signs all share the same visual properties without duplicating geometry. A common misconception is that a Material contains geometry; it does not. Mesh data and material data are separate so artists and engineers can optimize each independently. A concrete example you will practice is creating a material named M_PBR_Cube and assigning an Albedo and Normal map. The value of this separation is reuse and iteration. When you tweak a material property, every object using that material updates, which saves time and keeps visuals consistent. Takeaway: Materials are reusable surface descriptions that control shading, not models themselves. What Is a Material in Unity? means materials define color and light response, and are applied to meshes via the mesh renderer.. In practical terms, a material defines how a surface responds to light and texture maps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › What Is a Material?
Definition
A Material is an asset that defines surface appearance and how light interacts with that surface. It contains shader selection and texture slots rather than geometry.
Why this matters
  • Enables reuse across multiple objects for consistent visuals.
  • Separates art iteration from geometry editing.
  • Allows shader-based control of reflections, roughness, and detail.
Key Takeaway

Materials are reusable surface definitions that control shading and texture mapping, not geometry.

Concrete Example
Create M_PBR_Cube in Assets/Art/Materials, assign an Albedo and Normal map, then drag the material onto a cube. The cube's Mesh Renderer uses the material to determine its visible surface.
Reuse: One material, many crates
Iteration: tweak smoothness centrally
Common misconception: Materials do not add vertex positions or polygons. Normal maps fake detail without changing geometry; that is a material effect, not a mesh change.

screens.title: Creating and Assigning a Material
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and applying a Material in Unity is a short but precise workflow you will repeat often. Start in the Project window inside Assets/Art/Materials, right-click and choose Create > Material. Name the new asset clearly, for example M_PBR_Cube. Next, select the material to open its Inspector where you choose the shader and assign texture slots. For a Standard Shader PBR workflow, you will plug in Albedo, Metallic, Normal, and Smoothness maps. To assign textures, drag them from the Project window into the corresponding slots or click the circular picker. Once configured, apply the material by dragging it onto a GameObject in the Scene or placing it on the Mesh Renderer component's Material slot in the Inspector. A useful tip is to keep a preview object in the Scene, like a cube, to see live updates as you tweak sliders. A misconception to watch for is thinking assignment changes the mesh; it only changes the material reference on the Mesh Renderer. Practice this process until you can perform each step confidently and explain why each import or slot matters. Creating and Assigning a Material means create material asset, configure shader and texture slots, then assign to mesh renderer to change object appearance.. In practical terms, step-by-step workflow from asset creation to scene assignment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Physically Based Rendering (PBR)
screens.narratorSegment: Physically Based Rendering is a shading approach that models how light behaves with materials using physical properties rather than arbitrary artist-only settings. The core idea is to describe surfaces with measurable traits like metallicness and microfacet smoothness so the same material responds predictably under different lights. For an artist, this means focusing on real-world characteristics; for example, a metal surface is characterized by a metallic value of one and its color comes from reflections rather than diffuse albedo. A practical example: a painted metal sign versus raw steel. Both may share similar color tones but will react differently when sunlight or ambient light changes because metallic and smoothness differ. A common misconception is that PBR removes artistic control. It does not. PBR constrains values to physical ranges, but you still choose textures and tweak sliders to reach a desired look. The advantage is consistency; materials crafted under PBR look plausible in multiple environments and reduce surprises during lighting changes. Consider PBR a shared vocabulary between artists and engines that makes realistic results repeatable. Physically Based Rendering (PBR) means pbr uses physical properties so materials behave reliably under varied lighting and environments.. In practical terms, why pbr matters and how it models real-world materials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › PBR Overview
PBR Principles
Physical properties: Metallic and Smoothness define reflection type and clarity.
Energy conservation: surfaces do not reflect more light than they receive, keeping shading believable.
Material separation: diffuse color and reflectivity are controlled independently for realism.
Concrete Example
Compare a painted metal and bare metal. Painted metal has Metallic = 0, Smoothness high, and a visible diffuse color. Bare metal has Metallic = 1 and its color primarily appears in reflections.
Consistency across lights
Predictable artist controls
Misconception: PBR is not a single look. It is a framework for representing different materials accurately and still allows creative control.

screens.title: Standard Shader Properties
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Standard Shader exposes the core PBR properties you will use most often. Albedo is the base color and defines the diffuse reflection for non-metallic surfaces. Metallic is a 0 to 1 slider or map that determines whether reflections behave like metal or non-metal. Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred reflections appear, essentially the glossiness of the surface. A Normal map simulates small-scale surface detail by modifying surface normals without adding geometry. Finally, an Ambient Occlusion map darkens crevices and simulates soft shadowing from ambient light. A helpful concrete comparison: a wooden crate typically uses an Albedo texture, Metallic = 0, Smoothness low to moderate, and can use a Normal map for grain. A steel beam uses an Albedo close to neutral, Metallic = 1, Smoothness moderate depending on polish, and a Normal map for dents. Common mistakes include supplying Roughness maps without inverting them when a shader expects Smoothness, or forgetting to mark Normal textures as Normal type. Understanding the role of each property lets you mix maps and sliders effectively to reach the desired surface quality. Standard Shader Properties means each standard shader property contributes a distinct aspect of the final surface: color, type of reflection, clarity of reflection, microdetail, and ambient shadowing.. In practical terms, albedo, metallic, smoothness, normal and occlusion compared. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Standard Shader
Property Comparison
Albedo
Base color map defining diffuse appearance for non-metals.
Metallic
0 means dielectric, 1 means metal; changes how reflections are colored.
Smoothness
Controls glossiness. Smoothness = 1 yields sharp reflections; 0 yields matte surfaces.
Normal Map
Fakes bumps and fine detail by changing surface normals without adding polygons.
Occlusion
AO darkens crevices for perceived depth from ambient lighting.
Example Pairings
Wood: Albedo texture + Metallic 0 + Normal for grain + Smoothness low. Metal: Neutral Albedo + Metallic 1 + Normal for dents + Smoothness per polish.
Common mistake: using a Roughness map without inverting it for Smoothness sliders. Check shader expectations and invert if necessary.

screens.title: Albedo and Color Maps
screens.narratorSegment: The Albedo map, often called Base Color or Diffuse map, supplies the visible color details of a surface. For non-metallic surfaces, the Albedo directly represents what you see when light hits the object. For metallic surfaces the Albedo often contributes to the tint of reflections, but not to diffuse shading in the same way. A concrete example: a painted wood plank uses an Albedo texture with paint chips and grain; these colors drive the perceived material. When preparing Albedo textures, ensure they are saved with normal sRGB color space because they are color data. A common misconception is to use AO baked into the Albedo; keep Ambient Occlusion in its own map so you can control its influence independently. Also avoid putting lighting information like baked shadows into Albedo unless that is intentional for stylized assets. Correct Albedo usage makes it easier to reuse textures across different lighting and keeps PBR workflows clean and flexible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Albedo Maps
What Albedo Does
Albedo defines base colors and patterns. Keep it free of baked lighting and use sRGB color space on import.
Use clean color data for tint and detail.
Avoid baked shadows unless stylized.
Concrete Example
A painted metal panel uses an Albedo with paint chips. The same Albedo on a non-metal will show diffuse color; on a metal it mostly tints reflections.
Mnemonic: Albedo = "appearance color". Store separately from AO and other masks to preserve control.

screens.title: Metallic Property and Metallic Maps
screens.narratorSegment: The Metallic property determines whether a surface behaves like a metal or a dielectric. In practical terms, Metallic is typically a binary choice in PBR: 0 for non-metal (dielectric) and 1 for metal. Metals reflect light differently; they lack diffuse color and their reflections are tinted by the metal's properties. You can use a single slider for simple objects or a Metallic texture map for mixed materials, where white indicates metal and black indicates non-metal. For example, a mixed object like a weapon may have metallic rivets and a wooden handle; a Metallic map lets those parts be metallic while the rest remains dielectric. A common pitfall is using intermediate metallic values on materials that should be purely metal or purely dielectric. That can produce physically implausible behavior. When in doubt, use 0 or 1 and rely on texture masks for fine detail. This approach yields more predictable and correct reflections across lighting setups. Metallic Property and Metallic Maps means use 0 or 1 for physical accuracy; maps allow per-pixel metal/non-metal control for mixed materials.. In practical terms, how metallicness changes reflection type and color. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Metallic
Concept
Metallic controls whether reflections come from metal-like behavior or dielectric scattering. Metals generally have no diffuse component and color their reflections.
Practical rule: prefer 0 or 1 for physical accuracy. Use a Metallic map for mixed surfaces like metal screws on a plastic body.
Example
A tool: metallic rivets map to white in a Metallic texture while the handle stays black. This per-pixel control produces correct reflections on rivets and normal diffuse shading on the handle.
Mistake to avoid: mid-range values for primarily metal or non-metal parts cause unrealistic shading. Use masks instead of blended metallic values where physical accuracy is needed.

screens.title: Smoothness and Roughness Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred reflections appear on a surface. A smoothness of one yields mirror-like reflections, while zero yields very rough, matte surfaces that scatter light. Artists commonly work with either Smoothness maps or Roughness maps. Roughness maps describe the inverse concept, where roughness equals one minus smoothness. Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Smoothness vs Roughness
How it works
Smoothness determines the spread of specular highlights. High smoothness produces crisp highlights and reflections; low smoothness produces broad, soft highlights.
If you only have a Roughness map, invert it to produce a Smoothness map or enable invert on import where available.
Example & Pitfall
Polished marble: Smoothness high. Weathered concrete: Smoothness low. Pitfall: plugging roughness directly into a smoothness slot gives the inverse look.
Common Mistake

Do not forget to invert Roughness maps when using a Smoothness channel; check import options or shader settings.

screens.title: Normal Maps and Import Settings
screens.narratorSegment: Normal maps simulate small-scale bumps and grooves by modifying normals used in lighting calculations. They are powerful because they add apparent surface detail without increasing polygon count. When you import a Normal map into Unity, you must set its Texture Type to Normal Map in the Inspector so Unity processes the file correctly. If you forget this, the engine treats the image as color data and the surface lighting will look incorrect, producing strange artifacts. A concrete example is a brick wall where the Normal map provides mortar depth and stone relief while the mesh stays low-poly. The common mistake is the one described in the assessment: keeping Normal maps as Default. Fix it by selecting the texture, changing Texture Type to Normal Map, and clicking Apply. Another important step is ensuring the Normal map was authored in tangent space if your pipeline expects that. Key takeaway: correct import settings are as important as the texture itself for accurate shading. It changes normal vectors per-pixel to fake bumps, dents, and fine detail for lighting without adding geometry.

screens.title: Ambient Occlusion (AO) and Occlusion Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Ambient Occlusion maps simulate soft shadowing where ambient light is blocked, such as crevices, seams, and tight corners. AO does not replace real shadowing from direct lights, but it adds subtle depth and helps small features read better at a glance. Typically you plug AO into the Occlusion slot of the Standard Shader or combine it with a mask channel. For a practical example, imagine a rusted metal panel: AO darkens seams between plates and enhances the perception of grime. A common misconception is that AO alone will make an object look lit; it is only a multiplier for ambient light and should be used with caution. Also remember AO is non-color data, so when importing set sRGB off if the engine provides a non-color or mask option. Keep AO separate from Albedo so you can tune its influence independently and avoid baked lighting conflicts. screens.title: Hands-on: Create and Apply a PBR Material
screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on walkthrough you will create a PBR material and apply it to a cube to observe the effects of each texture and slider. Begin by creating a cube named PBR_Cube and place it at zero on X and Z and one unit on Y. In the Project window, add your Albedo, Normal, Metallic, and Roughness textures to Assets/Art/Textures. Import step: select the Normal texture and set Texture Type to Normal Map, then click Apply. For Roughness maps that are inverted relative to Smoothness, either invert the image or enable invert smoothness on import. Next, create a material in Assets/Art/Materials named M_PBR_Cube. In the Inspector for the material, assign Albedo, Metallic, Normal, and Smoothness (or inverted Roughness) into their slots. Adjust tiling if the pattern looks stretched. Finally, drag M_PBR_Cube onto the PBR_Cube. Observe how changing Metallic from 0 to 1 changes reflection behavior and how Smoothness sharpens or blurs highlights. Watch for the common mistake of an untyped Normal map and fix it by re-importing. Practice these steps until you can explain why each import or slider affects the final look.

fullNarratorScript:
In this short unit we will build a practical understanding of Materials and Textures in Unity and why they matter for visual fidelity. Materials act as the skin for your 3D meshes and define how light interacts with each surface. You will see how Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, relies on physical properties like metallicness and smoothness to produce consistent results across lighting setups. We will also cover the key texture maps used in PBR — Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness or Roughness, Normal, and Ambient Occlusion — and how to import and assign them correctly. A concrete example you will practice is creating a PBR material for a cube, importing a Normal map and setting its texture type correctly so the surface shading reads properly. A common mistake to avoid is leaving a Normal map as a default texture type, which breaks lighting. By the end you will be able to configure the Standard Shader and apply materials so your assets react correctly to light. Ready to explore material properties and practice a hands-on setup?

These objectives focus on practical skills and conceptual understanding you need to make PBR materials in Unity. First, you will be able to define a Material and explain its role in rendering. That helps you reason about why geometry and surface data are separate. Second, you will create and assign Materials in the Project and Scene, which is the hands-on workflow for applying looks to models. Third, you will understand PBR core principles like metallic and smoothness so your materials behave consistently across lights. And fourth, you will import and configure texture maps correctly, especially Normal maps which require a specific texture type. Each objective pairs a clear task with why it matters in a production pipeline. Practicing these skills reduces visual bugs, speeds iteration, and ensures assets look correct in different lighting. As you work through the exercises, check off each milestone when you can both perform and explain the step.

This second objectives screen lists the practical tasks you will perform and why each one matters to an art pipeline. You will prepare texture assets and adjust import settings so Unity interprets Normal and non-color maps correctly. You will create a Material asset, assign textures to Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, and Normal slots, and tweak tiling and smoothness sliders. You will then apply the Material to a cube and observe real-time changes as you move sliders to see the visual difference. These skills are important because they are repeatable steps used when authoring assets for many scenes and platforms. A deliberate checklist helps you avoid common mistakes like using a Roughness map without inverting it or leaving Normal maps untyped. Treat each objective as both a manual operation and a concept you can explain — that combination ensures you can onboard others and maintain consistent visuals across a project.

A Material in Unity is an asset that describes surface appearance by defining how light interacts with a mesh. Think of the mesh as the shape and the material as the skin: one provides geometry, the other provides color, reflectivity, and micro-detail. A clear definition helps you separate responsibilities in an art pipeline. For example, the same wood texture material can be applied to many models so a set of crates, fences, and signs all share the same visual properties without duplicating geometry. A common misconception is that a Material contains geometry; it does not. Mesh data and material data are separate so artists and engineers can optimize each independently. A concrete example you will practice is creating a material named M_PBR_Cube and assigning an Albedo and Normal map. The value of this separation is reuse and iteration. When you tweak a material property, every object using that material updates, which saves time and keeps visuals consistent. Takeaway: Materials are reusable surface descriptions that control shading, not models themselves. Creating and applying a Material in Unity is a short but precise workflow you will repeat often. Start in the Project window inside Assets/Art/Materials, right-click and choose Create > Material. Name the new asset clearly, for example M_PBR_Cube. Next, select the material to open its Inspector where you choose the shader and assign texture slots. For a Standard Shader PBR workflow, you will plug in Albedo, Metallic, Normal, and Smoothness maps. To assign textures, drag them from the Project window into the corresponding slots or click the circular picker. Once configured, apply the material by dragging it onto a GameObject in the Scene or placing it on the Mesh Renderer component's Material slot in the Inspector. A useful tip is to keep a preview object in the Scene, like a cube, to see live updates as you tweak sliders. A misconception to watch for is thinking assignment changes the mesh; it only changes the material reference on the Mesh Renderer. Practice this process until you can perform each step confidently and explain why each import or slot matters. Physically Based Rendering is a shading approach that models how light behaves with materials using physical properties rather than arbitrary artist-only settings. The core idea is to describe surfaces with measurable traits like metallicness and microfacet smoothness so the same material responds predictably under different lights. For an artist, this means focusing on real-world characteristics; for example, a metal surface is characterized by a metallic value of one and its color comes from reflections rather than diffuse albedo. A practical example: a painted metal sign versus raw steel. Both may share similar color tones but will react differently when sunlight or ambient light changes because metallic and smoothness differ. A common misconception is that PBR removes artistic control. It does not. PBR constrains values to physical ranges, but you still choose textures and tweak sliders to reach a desired look. The advantage is consistency; materials crafted under PBR look plausible in multiple environments and reduce surprises during lighting changes. Consider PBR a shared vocabulary between artists and engines that makes realistic results repeatable. Unity's Standard Shader exposes the core PBR properties you will use most often. Albedo is the base color and defines the diffuse reflection for non-metallic surfaces. Metallic is a 0 to 1 slider or map that determines whether reflections behave like metal or non-metal. Smoothness controls how sharp or blurred reflections appear, essentially the glossiness of the surface. A Normal map simulates small-scale surface detail by modifying surface normals without adding geometry. Finally, an Ambient Occlusion map darkens crevices and simulates soft shadowing from ambient light. A helpful concrete comparison: a wooden crate typically uses an Albedo texture, Metallic = 0, Smoothness low to moderate, and can use a Normal map for grain. A steel beam uses an Albedo close to neutral, Metallic = 1, Smoothness moderate depending on polish, and a Normal map for dents. A concrete example: a painted wood plank uses an Albedo texture with paint chips and grain; these colors drive the perceived material. When you import a Normal map into Unity, you must set its Texture Type to Normal Map in the Inspector so Unity processes the file correctly. If you forget this, the engine treats the image as color data and the surface lighting will look incorrect, producing strange artifacts. A concrete example is a brick wall where the Normal map provides mortar depth and stone relief while the mesh stays low-poly. The common mistake is the one described in the assessment: keeping Normal maps as Default. Fix it by selecting the texture, changing Texture Type to Normal Map, and clicking Apply. Another important step is ensuring the Normal map was authored in tangent space if your pipeline expects that. Ambient Occlusion maps simulate soft shadowing where ambient light is blocked, such as crevices, seams, and tight corners. AO does not replace real shadowing from direct lights, but it adds subtle depth and helps small features read better at a glance. Typically you plug AO into the Occlusion slot of the Standard Shader or combine it with a mask channel. For a practical example, imagine a rusted metal panel: AO darkens seams between plates and enhances the perception of grime. A common misconception is that AO alone will make an object look lit; it is only a multiplier for ambient light and should be used with caution. Also remember AO is non-color data, so when importing set sRGB off if the engine provides a non-color or mask option. Keep AO separate from Albedo so you can tune its influence independently and avoid baked lighting conflicts.
